items.q: Bounded blocking queue: how would you implement it with wait/notify and with Lock/Condition?
Printing in strict alternating order (print FooBar / print in order): what are the approaches and trade-offs?
Dining philosophers: which approaches prevent deadlock?
Read-heavy, write-light workloads: ReadWriteLock, StampedLock, or copy-on-write?
items.a:
ToolMechanismBest fit
synchronizedone thread at a timefrequent writes or a very short critical section
ReentrantReadWriteLockmultiple readers OR one writerreads ≫ writes and long critical sections
StampedLockadds lock-free optimistic readsextremely frequent reads and very rare writes
CopyOnWriteArrayListcopies the entire array on each writeextremely rare writes (listener lists)
**`StampedLock` — the standard optimistic-read pattern:** 
private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
//
public double distanceFromOrigin() {
    long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();      // acquire NO lock
    double cx = x, cy = y;                    // copy values into local variables
    if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {               // did a writer intervene?
        stamp = sl.readLock();               // yes => fall back to a real read lock
        try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
    }
    return Math.sqrt(cx * cx + cy * cy);
}
The fast path performs no memory writes → it can be much faster than `ReadWriteLock` when writes are rare. The trade-off is that you must follow the pattern exactly: copy into local variables, call `validate`, and provide a fallback path. :::warn StampedLock is not reentrant Re-entering it can [[r:deadlock immediately]], unlike `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock`. It also does not support `Condition`. This is the main reason it should not be the default choice. ::: :::deep - `ReadWriteLock` is [[r:not]] always faster than `synchronized`. Its bookkeeping costs more, so `synchronized` wins for short critical sections of just a few lines. [[o:Measure it]]; do not guess. - Writer starvation: the default non-fair `ReentrantReadWriteLock` can admit readers continuously while a writer waits indefinitely. `new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true)` fixes that at the cost of throughput. - You can [[g:downgrade]] (write → read), but you [[r:cannot upgrade]] (read → write). Upgrading is a classic deadlock when two readers both attempt it. - A write to `CopyOnWriteArrayList` is O(n) and creates garbage. It is ideal for listener lists that are populated at startup and read forever, but a [[r:disaster]] for lists that change continuously. - A copy-on-write iterator captures a snapshot at creation time: iteration never throws `ConcurrentModificationException`, but it also does not observe later changes. State that semantic explicitly. - Often, [[g:the best lock is no lock]]: use `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference` + `updateAndGet`, or an immutable snapshot swapped with a single volatile assignment. :::

items.q: CompletableFuture: how do you correctly make parallel calls, handle failures, and enforce timeouts?
items.a:
A common interview prompt: *"A booking page must call three services (pricing, seat availability, and promotions). How do you run them in parallel so total latency is determined by the slowest service?"* 
CompletableFuture<Price> price =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> priceApi.get(id), pool)
        .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS)              // Java 9+
        .exceptionally(e -> Price.unavailable());   // degrade gracefully; do not fail the entire page
//
CompletableFuture<Seats> seats =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> seatApi.get(id), pool)
        .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(e -> Seats.unknown());
//
// allOf waits for every stage; the subsequent join() calls no longer block in practice
CompletableFuture<Page> page = CompletableFuture
    .allOf(price, seats)
    .thenApply(v -> new Page(price.join(), seats.join()));
**Methods you must distinguish:** - `thenApply` (synchronous transformation) vs `thenCompose` (chain another future — [[o:effectively flatMap]]) - `thenCombine` (combine **two** futures) vs `allOf` (wait for **many**) vs `anyOf` (take the first to complete) - `exceptionally` (runs only on failure) vs `handle` (runs on success or failure) vs `whenComplete` (observes the outcome without transforming it) :::warn Three traps you must know [[r:Using ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]] (the default when no executor is supplied) for I/O work. Its parallelism defaults to `cores - 1` and it is [[o:shared across the entire JVM]], so saturating it affects everything. Always supply a dedicated I/O pool. [[r:Calling `get()`/`join()` too early]] in the chain turns asynchronous work into sequential work and eliminates the benefit. [[r:Swallowing exceptions]]: without `exceptionally`/`handle`, the failure remains in the future until `join()` surfaces it, wrapped in `CompletionException`. ::: :::deep - `thenApply` vs `thenApplyAsync`: the non-`Async` variant may run on [[o:the thread that completes the preceding stage]]. If that is Netty's I/O thread, you have just occupied the event loop. Heavy work belongs in the `Async` variant with a dedicated pool. - `orTimeout` (Java 9+) completes the future exceptionally with `TimeoutException`; `completeOnTimeout` supplies a default value. The latter is often the better degradation policy. - A `CompletableFuture` timeout [[r:does not cancel the underlying HTTP call]]; its thread can continue running to completion. You must also configure a timeout at the client layer (18-query-optimization.rewriting-the-query-reshaping-the-model.q4). - `allOf` returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`. To obtain the results, `join()` each constituent future afterward; that is safe because they have completed. - Failures are wrapped in `CompletionException`. Use `ex.getCause()` when classifying them; this is easy to forget. - Context such as MDC, trace IDs, and SecurityContext [[r:does not propagate automatically]] to another thread. Wrap the executor (for example, with Spring's `TaskDecorator`), or logs will lose their trace ID (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). - Java 21+: for I/O, [[g:virtual threads plus sequential code]] are often far clearer than a `CompletableFuture` chain (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4). Mentioning this shows that your concurrency model is current. :::

items.q: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore, and Phaser: how do they differ?
items.a:
These four synchronization tools are often asked about back-to-back because they are easy to confuse.
ToolPurposeReusableWho waits for whom
CountDownLatchwait for N tasks to finish before proceedingno — one-shotone or more waiters await N events
CyclicBarrierrendezvous N threads at one pointyes — resets automaticallythe threads wait for one another
Semaphorelimit concurrent entrantsyesthreads wait for permits
Phasera barrier whose party count can changeyes, across multiple phasesflexible
**`CountDownLatch` — accept traffic only after startup completes:** 
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
//
pool.submit(() -> { loadCache();  ready.countDown(); });
pool.submit(() -> { warmPool();   ready.countDown(); });
pool.submit(() -> { loadConfig(); ready.countDown(); });
//
if (!ready.await(30, SECONDS)) throw new IllegalStateException("startup timed out");
**`CyclicBarrier` — round-based simulation, with every participant meeting after each round:** 
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> mergeRoundResults());
// each worker has finished computing one round
barrier.await();     // the last worker to arrive runs mergeRoundResults()
:::deep - The key distinction: `CountDownLatch` [[o:cannot be reset]]. For repeated coordination, create a new latch or use `CyclicBarrier`/`Phaser`. This is the most common comparison question. - `countDown()` [[g:must]] be in a `finally` block; otherwise, one task throwing an exception can leave everyone waiting forever. - `await()` [[g:should always have a timeout]]. Waiting indefinitely in a production service is a recipe for hanging the entire system. - `CyclicBarrier` throws [[r:`BrokenBarrierException`]] for *every* participant when one thread is interrupted or times out. This is deliberate: without the full group, the round is meaningless. - `Semaphore` limits [[o:concurrency]] (for example, at most 10 simultaneous calls to a partner). This is a manual bulkhead, not rate limiting, which limits work over time (22.3). - `Phaser` is powerful but less common: the number of registered parties can change between phases (`register`/`arriveAndDeregister`), which suits multi-stage computations whose workers join and leave. - Java 21+: [[g:`StructuredTaskScope`]] can replace most "run several tasks, then wait" use cases more safely by canceling siblings automatically when one branch fails (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4). :::
